acceptable.choice: Keep C#/.NET on the isolated worker model, with startup tuning (ReadyToRun, a small deployment package, lazy client creation, reused static HttpClient/ServiceBus/SendGrid/ACS clients, no heavy DI scanning at startup)
acceptable.why: The team is strong in .NET, the isolated worker is the supported model going forward, and these changes cut the part of cold start that the language actually controls, without a rewrite.

acceptable.choice: Move these functions to the Azure Functions Flex Consumption plan with a small number of always-ready instances (for example 1–2, raised before planned sale days)
acceptable.why: This removes most cold starts at low cost, scales quickly to sale-day bursts with per-instance concurrency, keeps per-execution billing, and is Microsoft's recommended successor to Linux Consumption.

acceptable.choice: Elastic Premium plan (EP1) with pre-warmed instances, used only for this latency-sensitive app
acceptable.why: It has a guaranteed warm baseline and pre-warmed scale-out, so it is a supported way to meet the 2-second target, at a predictable fixed monthly cost for one small app.

acceptable.choice: Run the notification worker as a .NET container on their existing AKS cluster with KEDA scaling on the Service Bus queue, minimum replicas ≥ 1
acceptable.why: They already run AKS, there is always a warm replica, and KEDA handles bursts, so this is a sound option if the Functions plan economics don't work out.

acceptable.choice: Measure first: break down end-to-end latency (Service Bus delivery, scale-out time, host startup, worker startup, email/push provider call) with Application Insights before changing anything
acceptable.why: The 2-second budget may be lost to scale-controller lag or slow downstream providers rather than .NET startup, and only measurement shows which.

acceptable.choice: Pre-scale or raise the always-ready count on a schedule ahead of known sale events
acceptable.why: Sale days are planned, so capacity can be warmed in advance, which is cheaper than paying for peak warmth all year.

ruled_out.why: Go isn't a first-class Functions language (only via custom handlers, so the Functions host still cold-starts), Microsoft support is thinner, and nobody on the team knows Go. It doesn't remove the platform cold start that dominates.

ruled_out.choice: Rewrite the functions in Node.js/TypeScript as the fix for cold start
ruled_out.why: Node cold starts on Consumption are the same order of magnitude as tuned .NET isolated because the platform dominates, so this adds a second backend stack for a 120-engineer .NET org with only a few TypeScript developers, for little or no measured gain.

ruled_out.choice: Moving to AWS Lambda, Cloudflare Workers, or another non-Azure serverless platform
ruled_out.why: It breaks the requirement to stay on Azure with Microsoft support.

ruled_out.choice: Staying on the plain Consumption plan and relying on a timer-trigger 'keep-warm' ping
ruled_out.why: It keeps at most one instance warm and does nothing for the scale-out cold starts during sale-day spikes, which is when the 2-second target is at risk. It is also unsupported folklore and not a guarantee.

ruled_out.choice: Staying on or starting new work with the .NET in-process model
ruled_out.why: In-process support ends on 10 November 2026, so new work must use the isolated worker model.

ruled_out.choice: Native AOT for the Functions isolated worker as the primary fix
ruled_out.why: It isn't a fully supported production path for Azure Functions and conflicts with the team's need for Microsoft support. ReadyToRun gets most of the benefit and is supported.

ruled_out.choice: Moving the whole Functions estate to Premium or Dedicated plans
ruled_out.why: It breaks their focus on the cost of the Functions estate. Only this latency-sensitive app needs a warm baseline.

must_mention: The claim is mostly wrong for this case: on Consumption, most cold-start time comes from the platform (allocating an instance, mounting the package, starting the Functions host), not the language. A tuned .NET isolated app and a Node app have broadly comparable cold starts, and Go via custom handlers still pays for host startup.
The fix is the hosting plan, not the language: Flex Consumption with always-ready instances, or Premium with pre-warmed instances, removes cold starts for this one app.

A steady few messages per minute usually keeps one instance warm already. The cold starts that threaten the 2-second target mostly come from scale-out during the 200/s sale-day bursts, so scaling behaviour and per-instance concurrency matter more than single-instance startup.
Measure the real latency breakdown and current p95/p99 against the 2-second target before deciding anything.
Stay on .NET because of team skills, the existing stack, and Microsoft support. A second language for 120 .NET engineers has a lasting cost.

The in-process model's end of support (November 2026) means a move to the isolated worker is needed anyway, and Linux Consumption is being superseded by Flex Consumption, so the plan migration fits work they already have to do.
Cost trade-off: a small always-ready baseline for this one app costs little compared with a rewrite, and the rest of the Functions estate can stay on pay-per-use.
Concrete .NET startup tuning: ReadyToRun, a lean package, static/shared SDK clients, avoiding heavy startup work.

Check the downstream email and push providers (for example Azure Communication Services or SendGrid, and Notification Hubs) for latency and throttling at 200/s, since they can break the 2-second target regardless of language.
red_flags: Agreeing that .NET is 'too slow' and recommending a rewrite in Node or Go without measurement
Recommending Go without saying it only runs through custom handlers, has no team skills behind it, and still pays for Functions host startup
Treating cold start as purely a runtime/language property and ignoring the hosting plan (Flex always-ready, Premium pre-warmed)
Presenting keep-warm timer pings as a reliable fix for burst scale-out
Recommending Premium or Dedicated for the whole estate without discussing cost
Recommending Native AOT, or other unsupported or preview options, as the production answer
Ignoring the sale-day burst-scaling behaviour and focusing only on single-instance startup
Ignoring the in-process end of support, or advising new in-process functions
Quoting confident cold-start numbers as fact without saying they depend on plan, OS, package size and dependencies
unknowns: Measured cold-start duration and end-to-end p95/p99 notification latency today, and whether the 2-second target is actually being missed
Whether the apps run in-process or isolated worker, on Windows or Linux Consumption, and on which .NET version
Where the latency goes: Service Bus delivery, scale-out lag, host startup, app startup, or the email/push provider
The trigger type and batching/concurrency settings (for example Service Bus trigger with maxConcurrentCalls/prefetch)
Deployment package size and startup dependencies (DI setup, configuration, Key Vault calls at startup)
Whether 2 seconds is a hard contractual target or a soft goal, and whether it means enqueue-to-send or ship-event-to-delivery
Budget for an always-ready or pre-warmed baseline, and whether Flex Consumption is available in their regions with the networking features they need
Rate limits and latency of the email and push providers at 200/s
Whether sale-day schedules are known far enough ahead to pre-scale
